summary: Recommends that RFC 1643 be reclassified as an Historic document, and gives the reasons supporting that recommendation. It is an informational applicability statement and does not define new technology.

eli5.summary: This is a note saying an old rule book is out of date and should go on the shelf marked history, with the reasons why.

questions: what is the ethernet-like interface mib
subtitle: The case for retiring the Ethernet-like interface MIB of RFC 1643, which only covered half-duplex 10 Mb/s Ethernet.

tldr.problem: RFC 1643 (and its SMIv2 twin RFC 1650) defined managed objects for Ethernet-like interfaces, but only for half-duplex 10 Mb/s Ethernet.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement recommends reclassifying RFC 1643 as Historic and shows that no standards track RFC depends on it normatively.
tldr.outcome: New implementations should follow the updated specifications, currently RFC 3635 and RFC 2666, instead of RFC 1643.

today: RFC 3638 is an Informational applicability statement that obsoletes RFC 1643 by reclassifying it as Historic. It points implementers to RFC 3635 and RFC 2666, and it has not been obsoleted itself.

sections.title: Why RFC 1643 Is Out of Date
sections.content:
STD 50, RFC 1643, and its SMIv2 equivalent, RFC 1650, define managed objects (a MIB) for Ethernet-like interface types. They apply to half-duplex 10 Mb/s Ethernet interfaces only.

After their 1994 publication, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s and 10 Gb/s Ethernet were developed, and full-duplex operation at 10 Mb/s was standardized. Updates to RFC 1650 were produced to cover these, and they also deprecate some objects that are no longer considered useful.
sections.eli5: The old rule book described only one slow kind of Ethernet. Faster kinds came along, so newer rule books were written.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The memo calls RFC 1643 an obsolete specification, overtaken by events. RFC 1650 was officially retired in 1998. New implementations, even ones that support only half-duplex 10 Mb/s interfaces, should comply with the latest specification, currently RFC 3635 and RFC 2666.

The updates also require implementations of the EtherLike-MIB to support the MAU-MIB as well. The memo therefore recommends reclassifying RFC 1643 as Historic.
sections.eli5: Even if your Ethernet is the old slow kind, use the newest rule book anyway. The old one gets retired.

sections.title: Effect on Other Standards
sections.content:
The memo checks whether retiring RFC 1643 would break anything. It finds that no standards track RFC cites it as a normative reference. Five standards track documents mention it, and each citation is non-normative:

  • RFC 2020 cites it in a warning not to implement the EtherLike-MIB on an interface where DOT12-IF-MIB is implemented.
  • RFC 2358, RFC 2665 and RFC 3635 cite it to explain the history of the EtherLike-MIB.
  • RFC 2720 cites it only in an ASN.1 comment, which could be omitted without harming implementation.

The security section says reclassification has no effect on Internet security by itself.
sections.eli5: Before throwing out the old rule book, the authors checked who still pointed at it. Everyone only mentioned it as history, so nothing breaks.
